utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. While we are waiting for the witness to be brought into the courtroom, I would like to remind the parties that the Chamber asked them, on the 24th of June, to provide the scale of the maps which were admitted as D526 and P6599. And we refer you to transcript pages 22904, 905.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, therefore, if the parties have been able to verify it, and if there's any agreement on it, the Chamber would like to hear from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Let me just inform you that and Mr. Shin and I met yesterday and we agreed that we would do it within the next week. After that, we will submit our joint answer to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And apart from scales, then it's mainly also the grid to be found on those maps, because if you enlarge a map, you need something on that map that enlarges with the map or is reduced in size with the map because, otherwise, you'll not be able to draw any conclusions. Good morning, Mr. Radojcic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you again that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And Mr. Groome will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now yesterday -- I want to begin with going back to something that was raised yesterday. Yesterday, at your request, I promised you an opportunity to review your Karadzic statement to find when you used the term "encirclement" or "semi-encirclement," and just to remind ourselves what you said in this regard, you said at transcript page 23108: "As for that problem that we had with the terms of encirclement and semi-encirclement, if you can find my statement given to President Karadzic, I think it is the term 'semi-encirclement' that is used there. I would kindly ask you to do that in order to resolve this dilemma. I was in -- at the Military Academy I was a professor of tactics and I really doubt that I could have used the word 'encirclement' instead of 'semi-encirclement.' So I can only attribute this to an unintentional mistake." Now, yesterday I provided with you a copy of your Karadzic statement and can I ask you first: Did you have an opportunity to review it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And were you able to find any instance in which you used the term "semi-encirclement"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that the statement be brought to our screens. It's 1D02128.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now when can you see it on your screen, I want to first draw your attention to paragraph 4. Now, in paragraph 4, you make a reference to ABiH troops being deployed in an outer ring; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if we look at paragraph 6, in the first sentence we can see that you describe the SRK being "inside an outer encirclement." If we look at the second sentence, you refer to "the outer encirclement ring."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could be of assistance, the B/C/S appears to have those paragraphs in different order. 5 and 6 are interposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So with Mr. Ivetic's comment in mind, it appears that it's a different paragraph, so paragraph 5 for you and paragraph 6 for us. The third sentence of that paragraph reads: "My brigade was encircled throughout the war." And finally, in the fourth sentence we see you say: "The BHA corps that held the SRK in [sic] encirclement had more manpower than necessary." Am I correct in thinking that in light of your testimony yesterday, each of these references to encirclement is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And could this be corrected and made to read "semi-encirclement." I don't know how this mistake came about. If you look at a map, you will see that we were not encircled. My brigade wasn't, nor was my corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojcic, nothing can be changed in a statement you gave to other persons. It is on the record here now, and your testimony what your testimony in this case is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, yesterday in reference to this issue, you said: "I was in -- at the Military Academy I was a professor of tactics and I really doubt that I could have used the word 'encirclement' instead of 'semi-encirclement.'" And frankly, Colonel, I wondered the same thing. How could an instructor of tactics at the Military Academy misuse the term "encirclement" repeatedly, when it is obvious, as you have just said, looking at a map that was not possible and to misuse that term "encirclement" before two Trial Chambers of this Tribunal. Are you able to explain to us how that happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no explanation. Not a logical one. During the first time I testified nobody noticed that. I didn't either. I can see it now. I don't have a logical explanation. In my view, it could be a typo, and it is my mistake that I didn't notice that earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did anyone suggest to you that you used the term "encirclement" to describe the -- the location of troops in the Sarajevo area?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim categorically that that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'm happy enough to leave it there, but I will give you an opportunity if there's anything else you want to say about this issue before I move on. Is there anything else that you wish to, in fairness, say about this issue?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very embarrassing for me to find myself in a situation like this. I -- that in my statement it reads "encirclement," whereas one can see clearly that that was not the case. This must be a mistake obviously because all the other documents, all the maps show that we were not encircled. So for me to claim that we were would not make much sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So I want now to return where we left off yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could I ask that P6616 be brought to our screens, and this is the collection of several photographs. And could I ask that we go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you -- I'll wait till it comes up on the screen. You agreed with me yesterday that a turret could not be seen on the modified air bomb launcher which is the larger of the pictures that we now see. Do you agree with me that if, in fact, this launcher does not have a turret to move the rails laterally on a horizontal axis to change the bearing or the azimuth, that to change the bearing of the tubes or the rails that could only be done by adjusting or turning the wheels of the truck and moving the truck slightly backwards or slightly forwards?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak from my experience, i.e., from the experience of the technical solution of my launcher. Even without a turret we could move the aerial bomb and change the azimuth of its trajectory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. It seems that you are saying that your -- the error -- the launcher that was made by your brigade, it did not have a turret; is that correct? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the kind of turret that we saw on Plamen, but we had a different technical solution. There was a rail and the aerial bomb could be moved laterally on a horizontal axis, even without a turret. Our engineers saw to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could I ask then maybe to -- to help us understand this with an example. Let's say when the truck is parked, the rails are facing so that the launcher is facing due north. Now, if you want to fire those modified air bombs due east, how would the launcher be adjusted to do that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The launcher was not supposed to move that much, from due north to due east, for example. The vehicle had to be aimed towards the target and then the crew would make a fine-tuning or, rather, fine adjustments with a lever in order to aim the bomb straight at the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And so as I understand you, the truck is pointed in the general direction and then there is some type of lever which can be used to make finer adjustments to the exact direction of the rails.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, is there anything on the vehicle which allows the lever to be adjusted in a way that you know the precise bearing that the rocket is being fired, or is it done simply with a compass?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question precisely because really ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, the movement that you're talking about now with the lever would be a side-to-side movement; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And vice versa; i.e., from right to left or from left to right, depending on how you actually move the lever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when I asked you the vehicle -- was there any specific vehicle that you were to use, you said, no, but that it should have some type of hydraulics to change the incline of the back of the vehicle. Do you remember giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the most common vehicle that I'm aware of that has that type of hydraulic piston would be a dump truck, you know, something used to transport gravel and then used to dump that gravel out by extending the piston. Is that the type of vehicle that was used for the brigade's launcher?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to stay with aiming these modified air bombs. The launcher did not have tubes; correct? It was simply fired from rails; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, let's put the modified air bomb to the side for a moment. The rocket itself, it could not be fired accurately outside of the tube that was supplied by the manufacturer; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection. Calls for expert testimony and speculation. I'm getting the wrong translation. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic led substantial evidence from this witness on the operation of an air bomb. I'm simply exploring it. I think he is certainly entitled to talk about his knowledge of the weapon and how he used it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, in your view, could a Plamen rocket be fired accurately without using the tube?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't answer your question. Not in a very precise way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in a non-very precise way, what could you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I couldn't give a precise answer because my knowledge does not allow me to present relevant evidence on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say: My knowledge doesn't allow me to say anything about it, that is what I understand. But to present anything which is relevant, you can leave it to the Chamber whether your answers are considered to be relevant, yes or no. Can you say anything about it or can't you say anything about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I came here to testify, I wanted to testify about the things that I know well and on which I can tell you something without any problem and discuss them fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you are here to answer to the best of your abilities, give answers to questions that are put to you, and whether it's good enough or not good enough, tell us what your answer could be. If you say, I can't say anything about it; fine. Then we'll just move on. If, however, you have anything to say in response to the question that was put to you, please do so. And we'll then consider whether the quality or the relevance is such that we would give weight to it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to be fair and I wanted to assist everybody in clarifying the mystery of this aerial bomb. However, now we're talking about construction, about expert issues, so you have put me in a situation where I am invited to give an answer for which I'm not sure that it would be 100 per cent correct. Bear in mind that I was a brigade commander. I was never an engineer or a constructor in charge of crafting aerial bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just tell us whatever you want to tell us and if you say: I'm not completely sure but this is what I think it is on the basis of my experience, on the basis of my knowledge, please tell us. Don't enter into a debate with the Chamber. Just focus on what Mr. Groome asks you. Can you say anything about it, or can't you? And if you can say something about it, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only say that an aerial bomb launcher is similar to a Kacusa [phoen] launcher. It didn't have a barrel, it only had rails on which the aerial bomb moved. Kacusa was reputed as a precise asset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to be fair to you, this Chamber heard evidence that it was very imprecise. Any explanation as to why others considered it very imprecise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard from my colleagues about this bomb. Some of them were not competent. Still, they talked about the bomb. They did not have it in their catalogue of armaments. Still, they talked about it. And I heard them talk about the hole that it made as being 3- to 400 metres deep, which is absurd. I heard a lot of things that were not correct. I wanted to be a bit more precise because I had an aerial bomb and I gave you as much detail as I could, in order to help the Trial Chamber to resolve the mystery of the tactical use of that asset. I didn't want to dwell on the details of construction and some other expert details. I really wanted to help with you the use of that bomb. I wanted to tell you whether we used it, and if we did, why we used it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your explanation is that others didn't have the knowledge and didn't have the experience to -- were therefore not qualified to say anything about the precision. That's, in short, what I -- is your answer. Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Colonel Radojcic, if I can return to my question and, if you recall, my question really wasn't about the modified air bomb, it was about the Plamen rocket system. So let me ask my question in a different way. During your tenure as commander of the Ilidza Brigade, did you ever issue an order for someone to fire a Plamen rocket without using the tubed rocket-launcher equipment?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had the Plamen multi-rocket-launcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you have any rocket-launcher system?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brigade didn't, and I say that categorically. The Plamen rocket system, according to the establishment of the JNA, could only be found in operative units in the corps and in the land forces. Not as part of the equipment of tactical units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me put the question this way. Based upon your experience as a brigade commander and your experience as an instructor, did you ever hear of any rocket system being used, Plamen, the Orkan, the Grom, being used without the tubes. Just taking a rocket somehow and igniting the engine and letting it go. Did you ever hear of that as an appropriate use of a rocket system?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now yesterday you likened the purpose of the rocket tube to a mortar. Did you ever give an order for a mortar to be fired without using the tube?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be technically impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And am I right in thinking that it is technically impossible because it's simply incapable of being aimed if the charge is ignited without the fuse -- without the tube?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To put it simply, it is an entirely different technical solution. The principal of mortar is that you drop the shell into the barrel or into inertia. It falls, it activates the charge, and it is projected towards -- through the tube towards the target. The rocket-launcher tube follows a different principle. The tube functions as a guiding system that propels the rocket towards the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the -- the rocket-launcher, am I correct in thinking that the weight of the modified air bomb kept it on the launcher until such time as the rockets ignited and overcame gravity and off it went? Am I correct in -- in that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You don't know?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: okay. Now if we can shift -- as you remember now from yesterday, I want to go -- focus on particular aspects of this. I want to now talk about the temporary firing tables that you have spoken about. And it's your evidence that they were temporary or provisional firing tables for the modified air bombs? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now just to make sure I understand the concept of firing tables, am I correct that the firing tables for a Plamen rocket system would be different from an Orkan rocket system?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the tables are different for the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So every weapon system, every weapon that uses a ballistic trajectory will have its own unique firing table; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So if an expert technician were to create firing tables for a modified air bomb, he or she would have to make separate firing tables for the 100-kilogram bomb and separate -- and different tables for the 250-kilogram bomb; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And then separate tables would then have to be made for each configuration in use. For example, we would need three sets of firing tables for a 100-kilogram bomb that used the Plamen rocket, an Orkan rocket, or a Grom rocket. Each of those would require a separate firing table?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since these are different rockets with different ranges and charges, it would only be logical that each would have its own firing table.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would it also be logical - and perhaps this is an obvious question - that if one configuration of a 250-kilogram bomb used three rockets, three Plamen rockets, and another used four Plamen rockets, each of those two bombs would have to have its own unique firing table?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that we had the kind of launcher who could launch rockets with three engines. In the previous proceedings, I was mistaken when I said four engines. So I can only discuss my experience with the launchers launching rockets which had three engines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And my question is: If there was another system in use with a different number of rockets, that system would have to have its own unique set of tables; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, to create a firing table, expert technicians fired dozens of a particular munition until they can establish with a high degree of reliability its ballistics trajectory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, is it your evidence that given the severe shortages of munitions that the VRS experienced during this latter period of the war, that significant amounts of munitions needed to create firing tables were expended in order to create them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a question to be put to an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Well, last -- the last witness before you, Mr. Veljovic, just this week, at transcript page T-22949, asserted unequivocally that this were in fact no firing tables, temporary or otherwise, for the modified air bomb. Obviously you both cannot be correct on this issue. Is it possible that no temporary firing tables were ever sent to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Veljovic stated. But it is absurd to say that firing is carried out without any initial elements whatsoever. I claim responsibly that we did have temporary firing tables. They were temporary because the asset was not an establishment asset. The rest are my assumptions. I assume that no one would provide such firing tables unless test firings were carried out. What Mr. Veljovic said could probably be explained by his lack of knowledge of launchers and bombs. As far as I know, he didn't have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you -- I want to read you something -- a question that you were asked by Mr. Edgerton in the Karadzic case about the test firing of these air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this is at transcript page 31250 and that can be brought up in 65 ter 30850 at e-court page 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the question you were asked was: "Q. How many times was it fired? "A. If you mean in the area of responsibility of my brigade -- "Q. No. In testing. How many times was it fired? "A. Unfortunately I can't tell you that. However, if we received the so-called temporary firing tables, that means that those who delivered the firing tables to us had some relevant information based on which he was of the opinion that launching the bombs from launchers was okay." So my question is: Do you stand behind this evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In your answer in the Karadzic case, you used the phrase "if we received" when referring to firing tables. While I accept that you believe that you must have received firing tables, am I correct that you do not have a specific recollection of having actually seen with your own eyes a firing table for a modified air bomb?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the firing table pinned on the launcher, and I asked the chief of artillery about it. He told me that these were firing -- temporary firing tables that they used to direct the bomb and insert initial elements for firing. That is what I referred to. When I said "if we received it," it doesn't mean perhaps we had received it. I wanted to say "when we received it."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell me who the -- the name of the chief of artillery who showed you these temporary firing tables and explained them to you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think his name was Predrag Bosiljcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to please spell that last name.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: B-o-s-i-l-j-c-i-c. There's no E between the last two Cs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you didn't have temporary firing tables for mortars, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For mortars, we had standing firing tables in the form of a manual, and the firing tables or an excerpt was always attached to the tube of each mortar. It was a small piece of metal attached to the tube. It enabled the operator to enter the necessary elements in order to direct the tube adequately. It was simply done for practical reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now you've mentioned a manual. Am I correct that each specific type of mortar had a manual that provided information to soldiers about how to maintain the weapon, how to load the weapon, how to aim the weapon, how to fire the weapon? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Each mortar had its rules. No instruction but rules, the rules of 120-millimetre mortars, 82-millimetre mortars, or 60-millimetre mortars, which contained all information about that particular type of mortar. At the end of such manuals were the firing tables, and as I said already, excerpts from those firing tables were also attached to the tubes themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did these rules include information about which type of targets a particular mortar was effective against?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The rules also contained information on what type of shell is used by the mortar and one could target different kinds of targets with different shells. I can explain it in detail because when I was a very young lieutenant I commanded one such unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think for now this is probably a sufficient amount of detail. Did these rule-books also identify targets that a particular weapon should not be used against; in other words, say, do not use in this particular instance. Did it provide information of that nature?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no such information. What it read, approximately, was there are three types of shells for a mortars. Direct impact shell, which is used for open areas. It meant they exploded immediately upon touching the ground, dispersing and destroying an enemy force by shrapnel. Next, there were smoke shells, which could screen a certain area in order to camouflage our movement. For example, when approaching the enemy during an attack, then we used the so-called smoke shells. And there was a third kind. They were called marking shells because in the downward part of the trajectory, it actually had a small parachute come out and it would light up and show the area where the enemy was so that we could target more precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct in thinking that you had a standard rule-book including firing tables for each piece of equipment that you had in the brigade? So for your Howitzers, for your other artillery pieces, for each of them had you a rule-book with a specific unique firing table?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct. We had all those rules at our disposal, and anyone interested in the brigade could rely on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now you said there were temporary firing tables for the modified air bomb. Am I correct that there was no such manual for their use or operation? That had not been written?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it had not been written. Because it was not a standard establishment asset. You yourself said it was modified. It was modified in the process, and in order to be used, it required temporary firing tables. We discussed what temporary meant. What I wanted to say was that such temporary firing tables were to be used until such time when there are permanent rules in place, but the parameters included therein are nonetheless relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: At this point in time talking about the firing tables for modified air bombs. You said previously, and I quote: "I saw the firing table pinned on the launcher." Can you explain how it looked like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in detail. I don't think it was metal, though. I think it was glued on a piece of cardboard and attached to the launcher. I don't remember exactly, but I was really not interested in it at that point in time so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have been interested at that time because you said: "I asked the chief of artillery about it." Therefore, I'm asking you: What was the size of this firing table? You assume it was on a metal ground.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was an A4-sized format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have some further questions for you. Was is it handwritten, typewritten, or printed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Printed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many lines, approximately, on this A4? Was it ten lines, 20 lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I can provide an accurate answer. But the necessary elements were there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in order to operate the range finder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now tell me what the necessary elements were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to operate any asset such as mortar or, in this case, air bomb launcher precisely, one needs to determine the exact distance to target. Unless you have that kind of range finder, no precision can be guaranteed. The next element requires the application of an artillery protractor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you see on that piece of paper or metal, whatever it was? What did you see? Just tell me what you saw there and you are familiar --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I discussed it with the chief of artillery. We were some 20 metres away from the asset. I didn't approach it and check. We were talking about it, and I was observing their activity. I didn't go into any further details. I apologise, but I really can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in order to have an accurate firing table, even if only temporary, that you need at least a full list of angles of firing and the corresponding distances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. One must know or have a table and depending on the distance from the minimum to maximum distance. Between these two extremes, there is information in, say, 2:15-metre scale. The parameters changed every 10 to 15 metres, I guess, although I'm not certain. So the principle was minimum distance, maximum distance, and between them graded information. It included different elements. If one is targeting directly and the distance had been measured accurately, then the asset was very precise. If an asset is used indirectly, when you can't see your target, the angle and the azimuth, as we say, is increasingly important. We use artillery protractors to determine that and we need to rely on a compass, making it that much less precise. In any case, what we used was a laser range finder and we were precise in achieving the goal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The times you fired was direct fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was the -- more or less the range covered by the modified aerial bombs? What was the minimum, what was the maximum range?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't answer precisely. I know that there was a minimum and a maximum. I can suppose that the minimum range was between 5- and 600 metres and the maximum one was between 3 and 4 kilometres, perhaps. And I speak from experience. Although I can't be any more precise than this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to understand what you mean by that. So the whole range was, in your estimate, and let's take the highest, 600 metres as minimum range, and the shortest, 3 kilometres, maximum range, that is 2400 metres difference. Now you say a firing table would be for every 10 or 20 metres. Let's take the most, the largest one, that is, 20 metres. That is, you need at least well over 100 lines of tables, and that all on one A4? Is that what you're telling us? Let's be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wishing to explain to you as best I can how such assets are used, I relied on these figures. But as I said, we don't know what was the minimum and the maximum range determined. I was just trying to explain to you how it was graded in between. I said, conditionally speaking, that the minimum value was 600 metres and the maximum value may have been 3 kilometres. But I repeat: I'm not certain of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then, of course, I must say that I have seen in my life, in my present job, I've seen firing tables which are very complex and long documents. No way to get it on one A4. Therefore, I'm wondering, with your experience, whether you have ever seen a firing table for a -- such a weapons system just on one A4. That's what I'm putting to you and I'm starting with what you said from your experience you would expect, that is, 600 metres to 3 to 4 kilometres. I took the better side, 3 kilometres. I didn't take the 500 metres but the 600 metres. And I put it to you that you would then need -- that would result in a firing table which would take far more than one A4. I'm asking you whether -- you say it was just a guess, my 600 metres to 3 to 4 kilometres or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you take, for example, the rules of use of 82-millimetre mortars, you will see there that the firing tables contain several pages. But an excerpt of those firing tables is always attached to the tube. And it is not an A4 even. It is an A5, half the size. So the list is certainly incomplete. It is but an excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you agree that if you work exclusively on the basis of an excerpt, where there is no complete firing table available, that it impacts hugely on the precision of that weapons system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With a well-trained crew, the answer is no. Because, for example, they have the piece of information 2500 metres and 2600 metres, they use the protractors, and they can operate it to come up with a median value which would be the closest approximation to the exact distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said if you have a well-trained crew. You also told us that you were aware of modified air bombs being fired three times. Where did the crew get its training in firing modified air bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They probably took an active part, that is to say, their commander took an active part with working with the engineers who devised the contraption based on sketches, designs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the production of the system. But you would say working in a work-shop in constructing these is -- equals to the training in the field of the use of those systems when firing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what I wanted to say. I wanted to say that since it was done in the area of the brigade, the commander must have taken an active part in the making of it. So from the start, he was familiar with the details. As for the crew required for launching, it would have been an experienced crew with previous experience with Howitzers and other artillery assets. It wasn't a problem for them to engage successfully, provided they had tables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What happened with -- you were talking about three aerial bombs, modified aerial bombs, being fired. Did you have any others; and what happened with those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my recollection, since it was in the department of my logistics assistant, I think we had about ten such air bombs. We used three, and the rest were not. After the Dayton Accords were signed, together with the rest of the arsenal, they were transferred to Mount Romanija, in Sokolac, to the location designated by the corps command as the place where the arsenal would be deposited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have one follow-up question. You -- just a moment. You said in response to Judge Orie -- one moment. In relation to the A4 temporary firing table. "I discussed it with the chief of the artillery. We were some 20 metres away from the asset. I didn't approach it and check. We were talking about it ..." Earlier you said: "I saw the firing table pinned on the launcher." From a distance of 20 metres, what could you see what was -- what kind of metal was pinned on the launcher?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, before the crew prepared the air bomb for launching, I walked around the asset. I saw it for the first time and I was curious. Among other things, I noticed the firing table. Later on, I moved away, and while the crew was working, I discussed it with the chief of artillery. So it wasn't that I simply observed from 20 metres away. I had approached it before it was used. I wanted to see what it looked like because it was a novel thing, and then I moved away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Why did you say: I didn't approach it, if you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was around 20 metres away when the bomb was launched, that's what I said. And before that, I had walked around the asset. It's logical when you received something new, you go and see it, and then you move away and let the crew do their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm really not asking about logic. I'm asking what happened on the ground. On one hand, you said you saw it; on the other hand, you say: I didn't approach it. Now you say you approached it and but later on you discussed it 20 metres away. Did you approach it or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, I went close to it and then moved away. Everything I said is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may point out, temporary transcript page 18, lines 21 through 25, the witness never said it was metal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I look at page 18, line 23, Mr. Ivetic, it seems that you are right. I heard it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Colonel, in that last exchange, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, I see that we're at the time for a break, Your Honour. I'll make the correction -- well, Your Honour, it might be wise for me just to make -- I think there's been a mistake on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to go to the point that is raised by Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, for the witness. Now, at page 16, lines 15 to 20 -- to 19, this is the answer you gave, sir: "For mortars we had standard firing tables in the form of a manual and the firing tables or an excerpt was always attached to the tube on each mortar. It was a small piece of metal attached to the tube."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do see that the witness, I think -- let me try to summarise it. You referred to the excerpts of the firing tables on mortars being a piece of metal which was attached to the mortar. Whereas you said -- I think you -- you do not know exactly how it was attached to the launching system when it concerned modified aerial bombs. You guessed that it may have been something glued, cardboard glued on, et cetera. That's -- that's how I think your evidence in total now looks like. Mr. Groome, is there any matter you would like to raise in the presence of the witness or can the witness be released --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think the witness has been mis-recorded and I think it might sense to do to it before the break while it's fresh in his memory, if that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Colonel, I think there's been some misunderstanding on the record so I'll read Judge Orie's question to you and your answer, and then ask you to confirm or correct. So at transcript page 23, Judge Orie asked: "Yes, that's the production of the system. But would -- but you would say working in a work-shop in constructing these is equal to the training in the field of the use of those systems when firing? Your answer, the record records you as saying: "No, that's not what I want to say. I wanted to say that since it was done in the area of the brigade, the commander must have taken an active part in the making of it. So from the start, he was familiar with the details."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that, but I didn't say "commander." I didn't mean myself. I meant the chief of the artillery and the commander of the artillery from the ground. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's clarified now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break, and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojcic, we'll continue. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, yesterday you were -- you made a kind offer to provide or make -- make it possible for me to see this book that this French officer gave you, this memento. I'm wondering, given the novelty of the rocket launcher, is there any possibility that among your belongings you may have a photograph of the brigade's launcher or perhaps even a video of the brigade's launcher in operation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. Now that we're on the subject of the book, though, now that we're on the subject of the book, I wanted to say something, if you allow me. Maybe it's faster if I bring it while I'm still here, so then we do this through Mr. Ivetic, that I instruct him so that you would get it as soon as possible. I would really like you to see it while I'm still here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Since you are a sworn witness now, you're not allowed to have contact with anyone in the Defence, anyone in the Prosecution. So we may just have to wait until you're discharged and I'm happy enough to wait until that time to see it, okay? But thank you for the offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, Mr. Groome, if it could be realised through simple, practical instructions through the Victims and Witness Section, then, of course -- but you cannot have any contact either with the Defence team or the Prosecution. But, for example, if some of your relatives would know where it is, in what desk, in what room, then, of course, you could ask through VWS to ask them whether they could send the book with title so-and-so, located there and there, to VWS or to you here in The Hague. That is still a possibility. The Chamber has no opinion about how important it is or how -- whether it is important at all that we see it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, before I continue on, I just believe there may be something else in the record that you may wish to correct and you commendably have admitted where you have perhaps said something that is less than fully accurate. At today's transcript at page 11, you are recorded as saying: "Not a single brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had the Plamen multi-rocket-launcher." Now the Chamber has heard evidence from members of other brigades or one other brigade about Plamen rocket. The Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I refer the Chamber to transcript page 21204.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the Chamber also has an exhibit, P4404, which records the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as having used 390 Plamen rockets in the year 1995. So I want to give you this opportunity, are you -- are you confident in your assertion that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did not have a single Plamen rocket-launcher? Or did you mean just your brigade didn't?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I stated that my brigade did not have this, I know that with 100 per cent certainty the adjacent brigades, they didn't either, according to establishment. Quite simply, a Plamen is not supposed to be in brigades, according to establishment. It should be in operative units. As far as I know, even the corps did not have it. Maybe they got it from the Main Staff for temporary use for a certain period of time. But according to establishment, we did not have it. So that is an accurate answer. That is a precise answer, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now I want to -- I believe there's a contradiction between some evidence you gave in the Karadzic case and some evidence that you gave here this week. I'm going to read you both portions and then ask you to explain the apparent contradiction. Now during your Karadzic testimony, and let me just get the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During your Karadzic testimony at transcript page 31250, and this is 65 ter 30850, e-court page 43 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If could you pronounce the numbers at such speed that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that our transcriber is able to put them on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's transcript page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not saying that she did not perform surprisingly well, but just for future --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Future reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you were asked the following question and gave the following answer: "Q. So you have no information as to any testing that was done to the same exigencies as would have been the case in the normal arms industry of the former Yugoslavia? You don't know? Or to the same exigencies, pardon me. "A. Unfortunately, I cannot answer your question because I don't know." Now this week at transcript 23040, you said in response to a question Mr. Ivetic asked you: "Q. Did you ascertain if the launchers for the modified aerial bombs had been tested? "A. Of course. Not a single piece of armament or weaponry that is introduced into a military is introduced without previously being tested by the manufacturer. In this specific case, as far as I know, that testing was done at Kalinovik, which is an old artillery shooting range intended for such testings. And the firing tables we received were based and crafted based upon those testings." Do you see that there is a contradiction between those answers, and can you explain -- do you have an explanation for it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, I can explain. I think, as a matter of fact, that in giving an answer to the lady who put questions to me in the Karadzic case, there is a reference to Kalinovik precisely in terms of this explanation as to whether it had been tested or not, that's for sure. Please try to find it. I think there's a reference to Kalinovik because I gave a similar explanation there. It is illogical, it defies common sense to have something used without having been tested beforehand. I agree with you that the entire procedure was not followed here, as was the case in the former JNA, but it was certainly done because this air bomb was used across the heads of one's own troops, if you will. So any mistake would have affected our own people as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I direct everyone's attention to line 1 on the document on the screen, which is Mr. Groome's 65 ter number, where indeed this Kalinovik testimony is located in Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then we would need the previous page as well, because what now exactly was done in Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So Mr. Ivetic and yourself are correct. You did mention Kalinovik in Karadzic. So do you know this from your personal knowledge that there was testing, or are you drawing a conclusion because based upon your experience as a military officer, all equipment is tested before it is put into theatre.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second thing you said is correct. That is to say, I did not talk to these people directly, whether this had been done, where, how, et cetera. I'm just saying on the basis of my knowledge as an officer, I know that nothing can be used without going through a testing stage. In this case, I mentioned Kalinovik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can we move to the next page in the transcript. Let me see. Yes, I've read it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. The launcher that was manufactured in your brigade, was that ever sent to Kalinovik for testing?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did anyone ever come from Kalinovik to look at the launcher and verify that it had been built properly, according to the plans you say you were provided?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kalinovik is just a testing ground. It doesn't really have people who deal with this subject matter. The institute that constructed this, they did the experiments and then they made firing tables on that basis. And, also, they established the rules and instructions for building this asset. Probably my engineers from my brigade who worked on this asset, they probably contacted people from Pretis. So everything I know is based on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, what institute are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I used the word "institute," I meant a proper institution that deals with this. In this case, it was the Pretis ammunition factory. They were the ones who constructed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did anyone from Pretis come to the Ilidza Brigade after the launcher was manufactured to examine it and to verify that it had been built properly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any precise knowledge, but I know that they were in contact and that they co-operated in the building of this asset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome. Could you tell us something about what series of products, in terms of bombs and in terms of launchers, if you would know, in what series were they produced? I mean, you told us you had all together ten. You fired three. Have you any knowledge about the total production being 100, 50, 2.000, whatever would it have been? If you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are questions for the Main Staff. What the reserves were and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you know, tell us. If you don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- tell us that you don't know. And that would be true both for the launchers and for the bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for bombs and launchers in the Army of Republika Srpska, their exact levels, I really don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I now want to focus on the accuracy of the modified air bombs. And you state in your statement at paragraph 55, the average range of deviation for these weapons was up to 10 metres per 1.000 metres of distance. Am I correct in thinking that your evidence regarding the accuracy of these modified air bombs is limited to the three that you personally were involved in launching and that's from where you -- you've derived this deviation figure; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And am I correct in thinking that these rule-books or manuals that come with other weapons, that in those manuals there would be information about the deviation of the -- of the particular weapon?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give a precise answer. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: About suffice to say, the figure of 10 metres per 1 kilometre is -- is not information you received from Pretis or from any -- any other outside source. It's your personal assessment having seen three of these things go off.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. The experience of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, we -- we briefly talked about Mr. Veljovic, that's Major Stevan Veljovic, and it appeared that you were unsure what position he may have had. Were you aware that he was an operations officer in the operations and training department of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So in terms of the structure of the army, he was at the corps level, one level above your level, brigade level?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was in the corps command, in the operations and teaching department. As far as I know, he wasn't the chief of that department. He was just a desk officer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this week at transcript page 22949, Major Veljovic gave evidence regarding the accuracy of these modified air bombs and he testified that they could be off target by as much 2 kilometres. My first question to you is: You do recognise that this is a very significant difference from your evidence of 10 metres; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the difference is striking. And I wouldn't want to comment upon it because I don't know on the basis of what he said that. Maybe it happened in the case of some launches and there were such deviations. I don't know. I always say that in my brigade and during those launchings, that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He further gave evidence that this range of deviation of 2 kilometres was known throughout the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Is it your evidence, as a member of that corps, that you were not aware of this large range of deviation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that. To be quite frank, I wasn't interested in that. I dealt with the problems of my brigade. And if that is his statement, I mean, well, you know, that we all knew, I don't know how he could have thought that, that we all knew that. Maybe he meant the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: He also testified that because of this range of deviation, modified air bombs were not supposed to be used in urban areas. Were you aware that such devices were considered inappropriate for use in built-up areas?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The air bomb itself is something that is used in all armies of the world in built-up areas as well for engaging military targets. Please don't hold it against me if I give this example. During the NATO bombing of Serbia, these contact-fuse shells were used even in the very centre of the city of Belgrade, Novi Sad, so indeed built-up areas, and I don't see why this wouldn't be used in other built-up areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not going to debate the particular NATO example with you. Let me ask my next question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I would like to ask one question. Were the Belgrade projectiles, the shells, were they guided projectiles; or were they just ordinary air bombs as were modified in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course, those were the most up-to-date bombs with television guidance, state-of-the-art equipment, different kinds of guidance, and its tens of centimetres that are the standard there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that on one occasion - maybe this is a fourth bomb that was launched - that an air bomb fell on your positions but luckily did not explode; didn't that happen?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe you confused it with the first one that we launched that I talked about. The first one that did not explode, and I attended its launching. If that is what you have in mind, then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So the first one that you mentioned, it actually landed on positions held by your men. Is that how I should understand your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't fall on our positions. It fell between our positions and the cooling plant; that is to say, outside our positions. And just in case, for the sake of safety, I moved our people left and right. Because this was the first launching, I wanted to be 100 per cent sure that it would be efficient and safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me read to you evidence that Major Veljovic gave two days ago from this very place where are you now and that's at transcript page T-22956. "Q. Okay. I'm going to return to the question I asked you at the outset of today. Yesterday at transcript page 22956, you stated that Mr. Radojcic knows of one instance when a modified air bomb fell on his own positions but went unexploded. How do you know that Vladimir Radojcic knows of this one instance?" Major Veljovic's answer: "Well, I know because I was operations officer in the corps and he told me about it. "Q. When did he tell you about it? "A. 1995." Does this refresh your recollection of having told Major Veljovic in 1995 that a modified air bomb fell on your positions but did not explode?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certain that I did not say that to him. Perhaps he confused things. This bomb that I launched, if I talked about its launching and that it fell close to our positions, maybe it remained in his memory as a bomb that fell on our positions. So it is more likely that this is a misunderstanding or his poor memory. This had not happened. Had this happened, I would have mentioned this in the daily report, and you have all the daily reports and it's easy for you to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it seems that you disagree with his recounting of the conversation. Do I take from your last answer that you confirm that yourself and Major Veljovic did speak about an unexploded modified air bomb?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. That was 20 years ago, 19 years ago. I certainly don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Colonel Radojcic, in April 1995, can you tell us approximately how many modified air bombs did you have available for use in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly how many I had in April, but I know that I had a total of ten. I know that I got ten air bombs and that out of these ten, I used three. That's what I know for sure. Now, how they arrived, I mean, they certainly didn't all come at the same time. They did not arrive in the brigade at the same time. It is only my chief of logistics that give could give a precise answer to that because he is the one who dealt with this directly. I only received indirect information about this. When I would receive a report, I would see what the ammunitions levels were and then I would notice that they were coming in. But as for the actual dynamics at a given point in time, I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to say, was there ever an occasion when you contemplated using an air bomb around this period but you were told by your logistics officer: Sorry, we don't have any in stock?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I now want to address the -- the air bomb that fell on Hrasnica on the 7th of April, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move to that, Mr. Groome -- The air bomb that didn't explode, it was intended not to explode? Or was it by mistake that it doesn't explode?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our intention was not for it not to explode. It was an error on my part and the crew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. From where was it fired, the exact position? Where was the launcher located when you fired that bomb that didn't explode?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on the road between Ilidza and Sarajevo. For your information, it had been closed for traffic and it had not been used from the beginning of the war. So as soon as you leave Ilidza, the street forks towards Kasindolska Street and it is from that area that we launched this air bomb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And where did it land?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was supposed to hit a facility that is called Hladnjaca, a cooling plant. On some military maps it is marked. It is made of concrete, reinforced concrete, and before the war it was used for cooling meat. It's very big. It's dominant in that neighbourhood. There weren't any civilians around it because this is a place where there were only troops. And they were targeting us from there, and then I thought that we should do that first test by targeting that cooling plant. And if you're interested in details, perhaps I can repeat some of the things I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'll re-read it. Would be able on a map to locate exactly where you fired from and where the cooling plant was? And could you already now give me some idea as to the size of that cooling plant in -- was it 100 by 100 metres or was it 200 by 100 metres? Could you give us any indication as to the size?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly I can. I think it's about 50 to 70 metres basically. But maybe 50 by 70. And then it's about 50 or 60 metres high.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it was approximately at what distance from the firing position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think about 600 metres; perhaps a bit more, perhaps a bit less. But around 600.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it missed the target by how many metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never reached the target. That is to say, in order to be certain that it would hit the cooling plant, I asked the crew for them to opt for a lower elevation than the minimum one that is allowed because I was afraid that if it would fly over the cooling plant, that it would hit the inhabited part of Stupska Petlja. So I asked them to reduce the elevation so that they would be sure to hit the target. However, precisely because of this small elevation, the bomb set out and about 300, 400 metres later it fell on the side to the land, and then it did not explode because the fuse was not activated. But it was directly targeted, the cooling plant. That was good. It was sighted properly, but it never reached the cooling plant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was the experienced crew you told us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The crew was good. The commander was experienced. It was I who asked for them to reduce the elevation. It was my mistake. I admit it was much -- much of it was my doing, so it was not their fault at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this was one of the three occasions where you're able to form your opinion about the precision of the weapon system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was my first experience with an aerial bomb. Unfortunately, it was negative because it did not hit the target. Based on that experience, later we corrected our actions and parameters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, before you proceed, I really didn't get from your answer where this bomb fell. How far away from the target of the cooling plant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The bearing was good, but it fell before it reached the cooling plant, perhaps 100 to 150 metres before, but not on the positions where my soldiers had been deployed. It flew over and it fell so far away from the cooling plant that we could not come closer to it to inspect what had happened because we would have already found ourselves near the positions of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What's your best recollection of when this happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened before the second and the third launches. That was the first launch. I can't remember the date. But it was certainly our first aerial bomb launch. So if the other one happened in April, this first one must have been a few days before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your best recollection is it's a few days before the Hrasnica aerial bomb?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If the date that you mentioned was in April and it concerned Hrasnica, then it was a few days before, a couple of days, or five days, I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me ask you what is perhaps too obvious a question, but if you -- if you did, in fact, have temporary firing tables that, according to you, allowed you with your laser measuring device to calculate the distance, look on the firing table, know precisely where the bomb is going, if you really did have that, why are you deciding to adjust the elevation down? It doesn't make any sense.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in hindsight, no. However, at that moment, I wanted to see the effect of that bomb. I had not seen it before. And I wanted to do it at a distance where I could see it myself. That's why I ordered that to be the first target, but obviously the distance was shorter than necessary. The elevation was very low, and as a result of the earth's gravity, the bomb fell short. It was a small elevation. There is a maximum elevation and a minimum elevation, and obviously I actually decided to reduce the evaluation below the allowed minimum, if you know what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So your evidence is that the first time you deploy this weapon, you take it upon yourself to ignore the firing tables that have been provided and to essentially guess at an elevation to hit that target. That's what happened?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's go to Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that P592 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that between the time you let off this air bomb and then, a few days later, the Hrasnica bomb, you didn't receive any additional information from Pretis or you didn't receive any updated tables, you didn't receive anything additional regarding the use of this weapon, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from them. But I analysed the situation with my men. We analysed the mistake. We established what its cause was. And we did not really need any other instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I believe this is -- this is an order by General Dragomir Milosevic. I believe you're fully familiar with it and you speak about it in paragraph 107 in your statement. And in it, General Milosevic gives an order that: "The most profitable target must be selected in Hrasnica or Sokolovic colony where the greatest casualties and material damage would be inflicted." Now in paragraph 107 of your statement we see that you say: "The brigade to which this order was sent and I myself as its commander understood this order as an order to open fire at military targets." Have I restated your evidence correctly? No need to repeat all your evidence, but that's a correct assessment or a correct recounting of your evidence; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I want to test your evidence on this point but I want to get some details about what happened on the 7th of April. Now, under order, paragraph 1, sentence 1, we read: "The Ilidza Brigade will immediately prepare a launcher with an aerial bomb and transport the bomb for launching." Now, you as the brigade commander, you implemented this order; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I implemented this order. Just for your information, every aerial bomb launched was within the charge of the corps commander. I did not have the right to make such decisions independently.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Understood. It was a 250-kilogram bomb; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It had three Plamen rockets attached; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Each of those rockets had its warhead; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The engines -- there were three engines, but there was just one bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You gave evidence yesterday that the warhead could not be removed from the rocket, did you not? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Misstates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could you take the witness to his evidence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let me move on and I'll have one my colleagues give the precise reference to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can give you the reference: Transcript page 23143.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you would pronounce the numbers --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as slowly as Mr. Groome does --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Transcript page 23143. Mr. Groome never asked about the rockets. He talked about the bomb and the rockets and then used the [indiscernible] there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was: "Do you know if when they were attached" -- and we are talking at this moment about rockets being attached to air bombs for propelling purposes. The question that was put to you is: "Do you know if when they were attached that they were attached with their warheads intact?" Your answer was: "Yes. You can't touch it. It's full of TNT. You can't remove it and then return it. It's impossible." That is apparently what you were referring to, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for that assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, you've heard your -- Judge Orie read the -- how the transcript has recorded your evidence yesterday. Have I misunderstood your evidence on this point?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we were talking at cross-purposes. Namely, when you asked me whether explosive could be removed, I meant the aerial bomb, because it's TNT. It cannot be removed. However, when it comes to the multiple rocket-launcher, its rocket consists of two parts. It has the casing with the gunpowder which can be removed and the mobile part which is the part of the bomb on the rocket of the multiple rocket-launcher. That part had been removed because it was not needed to launch an aerial bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. You ordered only one air bomb be fired that day at Hrasnica; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And now your statement also says that they were legitimate military targets in Hrasnica and the two you mention were the Aleksa Santic school and the Hrasnica post office; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Which -- my light is on but I'm -- now I'm audible. Was one of these your intended target? Was one of these the targets that you ordered your men to aim for?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I ordered my men to target either the post office or the school because the two were close to each other. I believed that they targeted the school because that school was the training centre for the special units of the 1st Corps of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now is it your evidence that you believed that one bomb could destroy both of those targets or is it simply you left it to your subordinates to pick which one they wanted to fire at?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My artillery officers were locals. They'd always lived there and they were familiar with the terrain and the situation. They knew what would be easier to target, and they told me that the school was an easier target because the effect would be better and that's what they did. They targeted the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, why was the school a better target?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
