utterances.text: Because the post office building housed the command of the 104th Mechanised Brigade. Since at that moment, on that day, there was a combat ongoing, it meant that most of the command staff were engaged in combat, i.e., that they were not in the building itself. That's why we considered that we would achieve a better effect if we destroyed the centre for the training of special units. That's the explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could I ask one clarification. You earlier said that you ordered your men to target either the post office or the school because the two were close to each other. What's the relevance of the nearness? I mean, if the school would have been at a distance of 500 metres from -- from -- from the other target, what's -- what's the -- what's the relevance of saying that they were close to each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the two were close and they were of an equal importance for us. So I left it to themselves to choose what they targeted. Whichever of the two targets we had hit, the effect would be big. And I left it to my chief of artillery to choose the target, and he told me that he had chosen the training centre for a better effect, and he told me that it would have fulfilled General Milosevic's order better. And I agreed with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a long answer, but I have to establish that you have not given the explanation of the relevance I asked for. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Colonel Radojcic, although the bomb came close, it in fact did not strike either the post office or the school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we -- can we -- again I'm having problems with the audio. I can hear myself now. Can we please see Exhibit P591 on our screens, and this is a report for -- the report from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to the Main Staff on the 7th of April, 1995, the same day the modified air bomb struck.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe you've seen this already, but I'll give you a moment to orient yourself with the front page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And then I'll ask that we go to page 2. If we could go to page 2, I'll -- I'll read it to you, the part I'm interested in. "In Ilidza pbr, one 120-millimetre mine was fired and one 250-kilogram AB was launched at the centre of Hrasnica. According to the interception centre, the Muslims claim that the Luna rocket has landed." This report by General Milosevic to the Main Staff contains information about this air bomb that would have been provided by you to Milosevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This would have been based on the daily written, or perhaps oral in this case, reports that you would have made to your superior, General Milosevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that we communicated directly, so I could convey the information immediately. That was subsequently followed up by a regular daily report which was sent sometime in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to remind you of something you said yesterday and then ask you a question. This is from transcript pages 23120 to 21. "Q. Apart from misrepresenting, did you have to report on unsuccessful tasks; that is, you were asked to do something and your brigade was unable to achieve success in the task? Were you obliged to report that to your superiors as well?" Your answer: "Yes, of course. A few questions later I asked: "Well, let me ask you the question theoretically. Let's say there was a lesser commander than yourself who did fail in a task, would that commander be obliged to report the missed target or the failure to his superiors in his daily report?" Your answer: "Yes." So now my question is the following: Your evidence about targeting the school and the post office, I suggest, is not truthful. Because if those were your intended targets, given the fact that you missed them, you were obliged to report to your superiors that you had, in fact, missed the targets. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the rocket was launched, I received information what we had hit, from my observers, then from the international military observers, and UNPROFOR. I reported back to General Milosevic where the bomb had fallen. He told me: Okay, be on a standby. If there's anything else to do, I am happy with what you did. And that was the end of our conversation, which obviously I can only paraphrase. I can't remember word for word how it transpired, but this is more or less the gist of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As you've already just indicated a few moments ago, we have a awful lot of daily reports from the brigade. I'm not aware of you ever recording that you missed the intended target. Do you recall putting in a written report that you missed the target?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that it had to have been in the regular combat report. However, since the bomb fell some 20 metres away from the target, we believed that the effect had been achieved. Shortly after that, the Muslim attacks subsided, and there was no need to launch any more bombs. So it was only a relative failure. If a bomb like that misses the target by no more than 20 metres, the effect is still achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's look at this from a slightly different perspective and to do that I need to remind about your answers to several questions posed to you by Judge Orie. And this was recorded on yesterday's transcript at T-23122 to 23. "Judge Orie: Now, if -- and you hinted at the lack of precision of mortars, for example, then even if the first projectile didn't hit the target, then, as you told us, you would perform the task anyhow, so I take it that you would then do that by the second or third or the fourth shot. Is that correctly understood?" Your answer: "Certainly." "Judge Orie: Would --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- "that also mean that if an artillery projectile falls at a certain location, which is -- well, let's say, near, yes, which is near ... to what you considered to be a military target and if there is no follow-up hitting that military target, that then apparently was -- what was hit must have been the target. You understand what I mean? Because if where the projectile landed was not the target, you told us that you never failed to perform your task and then hit the target with one of the next projectiles." Your answer: "Yes." Sir, I put it to that you the reason you only fired one air bomb was that you were not aiming at either the school or the post office, but simply at the centre of Hrasnica, and the bomb exploded in the general area where it was intended. Isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, according to your own sworn testimony, if you had been aiming at the school or the post office and missed your target, you would have sent additional projectiles until you succeeded in hitting the target; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, misstates the evidence. As Mr. Groome testified -- and Mr. Groome read back the question, it was in relation to mortars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome. The question --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll await the Chamber's ruling on the -- I have nothing to say, Your Honour. This is happening now very frequently. I will rely on my question and the Chamber's ability to deliberate on the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may put the question to the witness. The objection is denied. Please proceed. Or let the witness answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And just so it's clear, Judge Orie, the first sentence: "Would that also mean that if an artillery projectile," not limited to mortar, and you said that you would send -- continue to send projectiles until you succeeded in hitting the target. Now, I put my question again. According to your own sworn testimony, if you had been aiming at the school or the post office and missed your target, you would have sent additional projectiles until you succeeded in hitting the target. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolutely wrong to compare an artillery projectile and an air bomb -- aerial bomb. When I answered Judge Orie, I had in mind a cannon or a Howitzer and an artillery projectile. An aerial bomb is an entirely different story. As soon as the launch was over, as soon as my subordinate told me where the bomb had fallen, I conveyed the message to my superior, who said: Fine, okay, I'm happy. Abort until my further order. And this is what I did. My superior gave me a direct order, and I continued to wait for his further instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, what we're dealing with here is General Milosevic tells you he is happy. You've -- aren't we talking about mission accomplished here? Your report to General Milosevic records a successful implementation of Milosevic's order. He ordered an air bomb be launched into the centre of Hrasnica. You did that. It landed in the centre of Hrasnica, mission accomplished. He was happy. You didn't need to do anything else. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection. Mr. Groome is again misstating the contents of General Milosevic's order. It is said to set it to a target in the centre of Hrasnica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- not the centre of Hrasnica. He is doing this time and time again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, Mr. Ivetic, what are you doing time and time again is to intervene in the questioning, giving clear clues and hints for the witness what your concerns apparently are with the questions, matters which you could have dealt with in re-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I take exception when a counsel misrepresents the contents of a document that objection is appropriate. I'm entitled to make a record of my objections. I'm entitled to have the Chamber rule on those objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I've made an objection, please rule on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic. You can make an objection. First of all, I gave you instructions about the objections yesterday. You didn't follow them. True or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, when it comes to documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is whether I gave you instructions on objections yesterday and whether you did not follow them at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe this objection is in concordance with your guidance yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- because I don't believe this adds anything to the witness. I'm talking about documents that exist, words that exist on paper, prior testimony. Those are not giving aid to a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic -- Mr. Ivetic, you answered my question. You believe it was in accordance with the instruction I gave yesterday. That's on the record. Any objection you make from now on, you'll have to announce that you make an objection. We'll then take the appropriate measures as far as the circumstances are concerned under which we'll hear your objections, and that's how we will proceed. We have heard the answers of the witness. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, would you please repeat your last question and that would include the -- well, it was a relatively long question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think Colonel Radojcic remembers the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, wasn't this the case that the task, the order that General Milosevic gave to you was successfully carried out, and he was happy with that? He was happy with the result. Isn't that what has happened here?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was satisfied with the precision. He said: It's fine. Sit and wait for further instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it is time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is time for the break. We'll take a break, and we resume in 20 minutes from now. The witness may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we take that break, could the parties try to agree on what portion of a clear map we would need in order to invite the witness to make -- to mark the position from where the first aerial bomb was fired and where it landed, and where the cooling plant exactly is located. If you could find the most suitable map for that purpose together, and I wouldn't even mind if either of the parties would invite the witness to make the markings as I consider them to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Weber has some proposals and we'll remain here during the break to discuss that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take a break, and we'll resume at 20 minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any agreement among -- Mr. Mladic, Mr. Mladic, I can hear you. You're supposed not to speak aloud. Have the parties agreed on a --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will work with page 32 of P3. I'm happy to do it after I finish this section related Hrasnica, if that's okay with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that there's no objection to that, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. Mr. Weber and I had looked through the map book, and we believe that that is perhaps the best choice that allows us to manoeuvre the map so as to get to the precise location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Radojcic, Mr. Groome will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that P582 be brought to our screens. It is a handwritten UNPROFOR report regarding the air bomb that landed in Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, while that is being called up, Captain Overgard, a witness in this case, was present immediately after the modified air bomb landed in Hrasnica, and I want to show you a report about the investigation that was done by UNPROFOR members after -- in response to this -- this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to page 4 in both documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm interested in the diagrams that were drawn, and they were not obviously translated so I will ask you to look at the pictures that I describe on the English version. So here we see a drawing of what they believed fell on Hrasnica that day. Now we have your evidence that the -- the modified air bomb only had three rockets attached. But with that in mind, am I correct in thinking that the diagram that they've drawn approximates the way the air bomb would have looked that day?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this drawing is neither precise nor does it reflect what it actually looked like. It looked differently. I do know that there were three carrying rockets, rather than -- rather than four. The drawing of the vehicle with the launcher does include some of the main elements but no detail whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I were or the Chamber were to permit to you have a piece of paper, a blank piece of paper during the next break, would you be prepared to draw a picture of what the air bomb that landed in Hrasnica looked like, a better depiction than what we have here?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very bad at drawing. I'm afraid I wouldn't be able to do much. I am more than ready to describe it in words rather than make drawings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I won't ask you to do anything that you don't think you can do well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome. Witness, you told us that there were three rockets attached to the bomb. Now that's clear. Mr. Groome hinted at that already. So let's just imagine this sketch not to have four but three rockets attached. Then you said: "The drawing of the vehicle with the launcher does include some of the main elements but no detail whatsoever." Okay. Now, could you tell us what is really wrong about it, as far as the main elements are concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that here -- I think it shows the armed 128-millimetre rockets, as can you see in the upper right-hand side portion. We can see some pellets at the top of the casing but in real life it was not so. They had been taken out. And all that was left was the rocket with its powder charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You say the warheads were removed from it, as we discussed earlier. What else is -- apart from there being four instead of three, what else is basically wrong in this sketch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The engines are too close to the warhead. The length of the rocket was bigger. Actually, the size of the modified air bomb was bigger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that, relatively, the length of the rockets is a bit too long here in relation to the size of the aerial bomb. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wanted to say that the rockets shown here are placed around the body of the bomb, and the impression is that it is all one large chunk, but in real life, they were removed. They were further away, and the air bomb itself and the entire device looked longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you say they were further away from the aerial bomb, what was approximately the distance between the rockets and the body of the aerial bomb? Was it 2 centimetres? Was it 10 centimetres? Was it 50 centimetres? Could you give us an indication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We see the rockets here placed on the bomb itself, around it. In real life, they were drawn back, and the -- they were fixed onto the bomb near the tail fins. This thing wouldn't even fly, as shown here, because the aerodynamics of it are zero.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, apart from your expertise on that matter, you say they were positioned differently. They were shorter, the rockets. Apart from that, they were with the warheads. What else is wrong on this sketch? On the basics, not on details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, basically the air bomb launcher is shown here with the railings alone, without any additions. But, as I testified before, there were levers which could move the launcher to the left or right in order achieve the right azimuth, as Mr. Prosecutor said. And they could also change elevation, depending on what was needed. As a whole, you can see the basic elements in the drawings, however, without these very important details. And I didn't even begin to explain the electronic system which was attached to it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Electronics was attached to what exactly? And electronics for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to activate the rockets, the charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ignition. That's what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Ignition had to be simultaneous because otherwise there was a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the trigger was electronically done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to page 2 in the B/C/S and page 3 in the English. And I want to direct the witness's attention to paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let me read you the -- or summarise the portion that I am seeking your comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart thinks it might be on page 1, e-court page 1. I apologise. So 1 of the B/C/S and 2 of the English. Okay. So paragraph 4 in the English is up, and -- okay. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 4 it states that the time of flight of the bomb was approximately 20 seconds and it left a trail of black smoke. Do you agree -- you observed this. Do you agree with that characterisation of the flight of the bomb?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not observe this launch because I was at the command at the moment. When ignited, there is a trail of smoke, although I wouldn't call it black smoke. The flight time, well, it should be around that. Perhaps a bit faster, not 20 seconds, but ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The report goes on to characterise the projectile being slow in flight. Would you agree that a modified air bomb travelled slower than mortars, rockets unencumbered by air bombs, and artillery shells?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And does it make or did it make a noise as it travelled through the -- through the sky?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It created quite a terrifying sound because during its flight and due to the emission of powder gases, one could hear a very strong hiss. That sound was not at all pleasant to the ear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And are you able to estimate how far away this sound would travel?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be heard at least 500 metres away, maybe more. My command was some 500 metres away from the place of launch, and I did hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The first projectile that you sent up, or first air bomb, that did you see, how far away was the distance between where it was fired and where it landed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 450 to 500 metres. If you have in mind the one which fell near the refrigeration facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's your evidence that this hissing, terrifying sound could be heard approximately a half kilometre away from the path of the air bomb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can we go to page 5 in both versions and I apologise in advance --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry, it's 4 in B/C/S and 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the report says based on fragments that were found, the people investigating this said: "We believe that the MBRL mortars had warheads." Now you have given evidence that they did not have warheads, so can I ask you to take a look at the -- their report as well as the fragments they have drawn and perhaps offer an alternative explanation to them regarding whether or not -- what they perceived indicated there were warheads attached?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. If it had a warhead where the powder charge was, it would not be preserved like this. It would have been completely destroyed. However, we see it rather intact here, given the fact that there was no warhead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. I'm going to now move to a somewhat different, although related, topic, so I'm finished with this exhibit. Now, Colonel Radojcic, in paragraphs 107, as we've already seen, and now in paragraph 88 of your statement, you assert that when General Milosevic issued an order to attack the town without specifying particular targets, brigade commanders knew that this meant only military targets. In fact, you say in paragraph 88: "All brigade commanders were trained officers who knew which targets could be fired upon." I want to now test this evidence of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could I ask that P923 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this is the document that you use in paragraph 88 to make this point. This is an order from General Milosevic in response to information that the ABiH is preparing some action against the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that we go to page 2 in the B/C/S and 1 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, as part of this particular order, there is a long list of tasks to be undertaken, and we can see one of them is underlined in the original and the English, which says: "Have launching pads and aerial bombs ready for firing on the town ..." Now, my question to you, as you point out in paragraph 88, is that he does not specify a target in this order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it's your evidence to this Chamber that this reference to preparing to send modified air bombs into the town should be understood by the Chamber to mean only known military targets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this document is classified as strictly confidential. This is a high level of security; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the SRK Command had the act to provide brigade commanders with information confidentially; correct? You had secure communications.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had secured and non-secured communication. We had telephone lines going across the airport runway and they were not safe. There were such lines also which went through our territory and they were not mounted to repeaters and, thus, they were much more secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I guess the point I'm trying to make is that General Milosevic had the ability to send you information in a secure way and be quite confident that the enemy would not get that information.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the first sentence of this order is quite vague and in contrast to other orders the Chamber has seen. It simply indicates that there is information that the enemy is planning something, some action against the SRK, without any indication of where or what type of action. Does this indicate that the corps command had limited knowledge about the specifics of the operation that was being planned by the enemy?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is merely a preparatory order. Detailed orders came as a follow-up. This is just in terms of preparation, so that we should undertake all measures, raise combat readiness, and, later on, a new order would arrive that was more precise. If you have one such order, you will see for yourself that I'm telling you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's take a look at another order and this order is just a matter of days after this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And could I ask that 65 ter 18618 be brought to our screens. It is an order from Major-General Dragomir Milosevic dated the 30th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to give you a moment to study the first page to familiarize yourself with the basics of the document. Let me know when you've had a chance to read that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'm interested in particular in number 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if we could please advance the English copy to the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now item number 10 reads: "Locations with buildup of enemy forces (the tunnel, Igman, Pazaric and so on) must be constantly monitored and targets observed attacked with precise fire." My first question is: Here, General Milosevic indicates the type of target to be engaged, locations with buildups of enemy forces; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And in addition to the type, he indicates three specific locations: The tunnel, Igman, and Pazaric. Were these locations where were there buildup of forces as you recall?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I can explain, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm more interested in the procedure than the actual events underneath this order so hold the more detailed description for a bit. So, in this order, he not only gives the type of locations, he gives specific examples to make clear his intention. Am I correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, let's focus on the phrase "targets observed." This means that before firing on the target, that is, the group of enemy forces, it had to be observed; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So according to this order, if you can't see the enemy, you're not to fire?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now let's focus on the phrase "with precise fire." By using this phrase, "with precise fire," General Milosevic left it to his subordinate brigade and battalion commanders to determine what weapon to use. In other words, he left it to subordinates to decide whether to use a cannon, a Howitzer, a mortar, or perhaps even rifle fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And he doesn't want a weapon used with a large deviation, a weapon which may miss the buildup of troops; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When one says "precise fire," it is understood that we are expected to target precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And would that mean if you are -- if you have a choice of weapons, that you are to choose the one with which the greatest precision can be achieved?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The best possible precision and effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we move the English back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I want to draw your attention to item 1. In fact, he also orders that: "Artillery pieces must be prepared for night-time action." So, sir, this included making sure that artillery pieces contemplated by this order would be -- were to be prepared so as to allow them to be accurately aimed even in the dark of night; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So I want to give you my understanding of the logic of this order and see if you agree. The logic of this order is as follows: There is a buildup of enemy troops and efforts should be made to neutralise them or at least disperse them by targeting them precisely. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So could I ask that we now go back to P923, and while that is being brought I want to recap what we know from this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, Milosevic gives the type of location to be targeted; two, several examples of the type of target to be engaged; three, leaves it to subordinate commanders to select the weapon; four, requires that the target can be seen; and, five, requires artillery pieces to be prepared so that they can be aimed at night and requires the attack to be done with precision. Do you agree with my characterisation of this -- that last order that we looked at?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now 923 is back up on the screen. This is the order from the 19th of April. Now, it's your evidence that the phrase "firing on the town" means military targets known to the brigade commanders; correct? Where he uses that phrase here.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Unlike the 30th of April order, in this 19th of April order, General Milosevic does not leave it to the brigade commander to choose the appropriate weapon for the target. In fact, he gives an explicit order that you prepare an air bomb, which, it is the Prosecution's case, is the most imprecise weapon at your disposal. But do you agree that in this 19th of April order, General Milosevic is dictating in the order itself -- you don't have a choice about the weapon to use. You must use the aerial bomb; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he just said that we should prepare air bombs for activity. That meant to prepare air bombs, to take up positions from where targeting is the most favourable, and this order does not exclude the possibility of using other artillery pieces for targeting different objectives in town in line with that explanation of yours. Selected targets, targets selected in advance, civilian ones -- no, sorry, not civilian ones, military ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Of the military targets that you were aware of, would you agree with me that a modified air bomb would be inappropriate for use with respect to some of them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly I could not hit all the targets that I had with that air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- in this 19th of April order, there is not only no mention of a specific target but there is no mention of even a type of target. I'm correct in that, am I not?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So now let me characterise what I see the logic in this order and let me ask you whether you agree. The logic of this order is as follows: We have non-specific information that the enemy is preparing for an action against the VRS. It's unclear what that is. One of the options to repel this action is to use a modified air bomb somewhere in the city. Is that the logic of this order?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of this order was that it was a preparatory order to raise combat readiness, to inform all officers down to the lowest level about the possible consequences in terms of what would happen if we did not do that. Then to prepare for night action. Then also to get ammunition. Quite simply to prepare for possible combat. So I understood this as a preparatory order. It is rather imprecise, I must admit. And without that additional sentence, military targets. Which certainly does not mean that when receiving this order I would have fired an air bomb or would have used artillery to fire at different targets without any kind of selection. And I'll explain later on - we'll probably get to that - how I would do the targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 18618.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 18618 receives number P6617, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6617 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I want to return to the air bomb that was launched against Hrasnica. Can I ask that we bring up P1048 and this is a report from the VRS Main Staff to the RS president dated the 7th of April, 1995, the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now keeping the differences between the two orders that we've just looked at, the 19th of April and the 30th of April, okay, now, the portion -- I'll give you a moment to look at the -- the heading. There's a lot in this particular report that I'm not interested in at the moment. Once have you oriented yourself to the -- the date and nature of the report generally, let me know and I'll go to the page that I want to draw your attention to specifically.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can move on because this is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's okay to move on, I believe, is what you're indicating.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we go to page 3 in the B/C/S and page 5 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I can ask you to draw your attention to where the bombing of Hrasnica is reported to Karadzic. Okay. And for the -- it's (b). It's 3(b). Hopefully that helps you find it. Have you found out?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And for the Chamber's benefit, it's at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it's reported: "(B), situation in the corps: The enemy activity was adequately responded to whereby an air bomb (250 kilogram) was launched on the centre of Hrasnica." Now, General Milovanovic, who authored this report, is informing President Karadzic that the enemy activity was adequately responded to; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The bombing of Hrasnica was a decision that was taken in response to something that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina had done; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So now let's go back to Milosevic's order to bomb Hrasnica and see what the enemy had done that had to be responded to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can we please have P592 on our screen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And this time I want to focus on not the actual orders but the situation that Milosevic seeks to respond to. So this order to bomb Hrasnica, Sokolovic, where the greatest casualties and material damage can be inflicted is in response to: "For the past three days, Muslim forces have been attacking the positions of the 2nd Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade, and the attacks are particularly pronounced in the sector of the Famos factory. Several of our soldiers and a large number of civilians had [sic] been wounded." Colonel Radojcic, I put to you that the logic and the motivation of this order, which I submit you fully appreciated at the time you implemented this order, was that the ABiH had injured a large number of Serb civilians, and the VRS was going to respond by firing a modified air bomb into middle of a built-up area with many civilians with the intent to injure a similarly large number of civilians. Isn't that the truth of what happened on the 7th of April, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to give a precise answer to this question of yours, allow me to say that, according to international law of war, the commander of a unit in whose zone activity is taking place is duty-bound to evacuate the civilian population in order to avoid civilian casualties. So the commander of 104th Brigade, Mr. Fikret Prevljak, if he intended to attack the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade, he also had to inform the civilian population that they should be evacuated. Or at least that they should seek shelter, in shelters, because of the forthcoming combat. He had not done that. That is the first thing that I wish to say. Secondly, I, as a trained officer, if I would receive an order to target civilians, especially with an air bomb, I would know that that order constitutes a crime and I would not have carried it out. This order, I must admit, is written very unskillfully. I doubt that it was General Milosevic who wrote that. It must have been one of his duty operations officers on his instructions. So when I am told to hit a target, for me there are only military targets. Anything else would constitute a crime, as far as I'm concerned. And trust me when I say that I would not have carried out such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But, sir, earlier today you told us that Milosevic was happy with the result of the air bomb. You didn't hit a military target. You hit a civilian target, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hit a civilian target. I did not hit exactly the facility that I had targeted. Now why was General Milosevic satisfied? Because of the effect that this fired air bomb had caused. It's not the losses that were inflicted. They probably concluded: If you do not stop, we will go on. So they did stop. So claiming that we wanted to target civilians, that can only be viewed in the context of the answer that I provided about the obligations of the commander of the Muslim side and my understanding of the order, no other way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask for -- you say he was happy about the effect. Now, when did he tell you that he was happy with that result of your action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After carrying out his order to launch the air bomb and when I received the exact information as to where it had fallen. I used radio communication and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it one hour after it was fired, two hours after it was fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Less. Less. I think about 30 or 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what did you report to him as being the effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I knew at that moment. So I did not know about the effects in terms of possible casualties. I knew where it had fallen and I said that we had carried out his order. The target was not hit, but it fell close to the target. And I asked for further instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were apparently informed in detail about where the shell had fallen, or where the bomb had fallen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment, not in detail. Because my observers from the observation posts saw where the bomb had fallen, and I knew the location as to where it had fallen, but I did not know of the possible casualties or losses that had been inflicted by the bomb. It was only later that I learned about that from the members of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you know what the -- that the school was located in the centre of a village or town, whatever you call it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a village. It's an integral part of Sarajevo, it's just on the periphery, and it is inhabited and it consists of -- yes, I knew what I was targeting. And I understood that, at that point in time, at that place there should be no civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because they should have been evacuated, is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I expected the commander of the 104th Brigade to observe international law too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you considered that there should be no civilians but did you verify whether there were any civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that there were civilians in Hrasnica and in Sokolovic Kolonija, which is an integral part of Hrasnica, a newer part, closer to the river. I knew that, but I also that I was targeting a facility where there were no civilians. So this was the centre for training the special forces of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you missed that target.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've said "yes" several times. But it wasn't that much of a miss, so it's not that civilians outside that zone were affected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us about the destructive power of an aerial bomb and this was a 250-kilogram one. Have you considered, when reporting about the effect, what the effect would have been on the houses and constructions next to what you told us the target was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I considered that, and I knew that an air bomb directly destroys a target. But it falls outside of that, most of its force is spent beyond. For example, I received information to the effect that if it falls 50 metres away or 30 metres away from a human being, the worst thing that can happen is that that person's eardrum bursts. So that is what I learned from people who are better versed in this subject matter. So the air bomb caused a crater there. The dimensions I already mentioned to you. It was 5 metres deep and it was about 15 metres wide, which speaks in itself that it was intended to destroy a building, not kill civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have a further question for you later, but I have to verify part of your testimony of yesterday. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Colonel Radojcic, maybe it will help if we remind ourselves of what happened when your aerial bomb fell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart now to play P839. It's a report of the BBC correspondent Martin Bell, dated the 7th of April, 1995. I'm playing at 17 seconds of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: "The cease-fire appears to be crumbling rapidly. Today there was offensives on at least two fronts in Bosnia and south of Sarajevo. The suburb of Hrasnica came under Serbian attack for the third successive day. A rocket levelled five houses, killed one person, and injured several more."

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, sir, from your earlier evidence that you expected the ABiH commander to remove civilians, does that indicate that you knew this contraption was being fired into an area densely populated by civilians? You just expected them to have been moved?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I had expected that because, in similar situations, when I received information or if activity of this kind would start, I would order people to move to shelters. So I expected -- since fighting had been going on for three days, I expected the population to have been removed to shelters, and it is only commonsensical. These are distances that are not measured in terms of kilometres but the distance between our lines is in the hundreds of metres. So, of course, I expected that next to the centre for training special forces there wouldn't be any civilians living there and it's only natural that I would have expected that. This just shows a fragment. I see that this was filmed at 2114; that is to say, almost 12 hours after the explosion. Now, whether that is that place, whether those are the actual affects, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it your evidence now that what we've seen here you believe to be false evidence or concocted evidence; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is too grave a word. I did not say "false" or "concocted." I am just saying that he hasn't convinced me that these are the affects of an air bomb. Don't forget that area of Sokolovic Kolonija, Hrasnica, and Ilidza, during the many years of war -- this is 1995. All of it had been destroyed completely. There were very few buildings that hadn't been damaged. On the basis of what can I know that this is an air bomb? Are there any remnants of those fragments that you showed me? Can we see any of that in this? When you show me that, I can believe this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps it's time to move from air bombs for a time. I'm going to go through some miscellaneous questions I have about your statement and your associated exhibits --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we move. I notice that you -- you do say that this video is at 21 hours 14 minutes and you say there were many destructions happening during that year. But this video is dated the 7th of April. Were there many such incidents on the 7th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for my command, the command of the Ilidza Brigade, there weren't any other incidents. There was shooting there all the time. We don't count that as incidents. There was always small-arms fire even when there was a cease-fire on, let alone when there wasn't. However, the thrust of this activity was on the opposite side from me. The 4th Brigade was between us. There was this corridor that leads from the airport runway towards Igman, so Hrasnica and Sokolovic Kolonija was between the two brigades of ours. On my side there wasn't any activity, and on the other side there had been intensive activity going on for already three days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that long answer. Can you please answer my question. My question simply is: Were there incidents -- many incidents on the 7th of April of similar magnitude; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 07625 be brought to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, paragraph 113 of your statement begins: "I was shown document 65 ter 07625. There was a meeting of the commanders of brigades or regiments and the independent battalions with the commander of the SRK." Now when I call up -- when I call up 65 ter 07625, I see that it is the shorthand notes of the 58th Supreme Defence Council meeting held on the 21st of November, 1996. It is clearly not a meeting of the SRK commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, we have documents on the screen which don't correspond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar tells me that there's no B/C/S version of this document and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- from what I see in my e-court system, there seems to be only an English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that there are two -- as a matter of fact, it seems that two times the English version is uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So this is a document that's being tendered by the Defence as an associated exhibit. I believe there's a mistake. So what I want to ask the witness is the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it is uploaded by the Defence, then I would invite the Defence to also upload the B/C/S version if there's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's a Prosecution document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It is a Prosecution document, but as I said, the paragraph 113 says that it's a document related to a meeting of brigade commanders and we can clearly that this is a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, just to be clear, you've never attended a meeting of the Supreme Defence Council, have you? General Perisic ever ask you to come to a meeting up in Belgrade at the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No. I was too small a person for that kind of meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So I believe this is an error. So take a look at paragraph 113 of your statement and my question to you is: The document that you were referring to, can you tell us what was the approximate date of that document so we can try to figure out what is the document that you describe in paragraph 113 of your statement. Again, what you say is there was a meeting of the commanders of brigades or regiments and independent battalions with the commander of the SRK.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You really have to familiarize me with this a bit more. I really don't know. There were so many meetings. I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can we have D535 on the screen, especially paragraph 113.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So perhaps the best question for me to ask you is: Do you recall now what the document is that you were shown and for which paragraph 113 refers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us the approximate date of that document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was approximately 1994, but I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you give us a month?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No. Do you know who the author was of the document?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this document was probably written by one of the operations officers from the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us, in substance, what the document said?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. As I've already said, within my brigade there weren't any professional officers. In addition to myself, there was only one more professional officer. All the rest were reserve officers who had completed reserve training, reserve officers' schools before the war, and that is where they were taught about carrying out high positions in the army. In addition to that, many persons figured prominently in fighting, and they were appointed commanders although they had not had proper training. I mean, I didn't have a single commander who had even completed reserve officer school. Would you please allow me to finish what I started? From that point of view, I asked the corps command that at that time of cease-fire, measures be taken for such officers to enrol in courses so that the duties that they carry out would be carried out in the best possible way. So that order has to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I may be able to assist. The similar text from the Karadzic witness statement refers to a Karadzic document which I have been able to locate, which is in our case Defence exhibit D00094, which had the Prosecution 65 ter number of 28501.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think the most appropriate thing at this stage is -- and I certainly have no objection to Mr. Ivetic re-opening his direct examination once I finish my cross-examination to -- to show that document to the witness to confirm. But certainly, as an associated exhibit, 07625 fails to meet the test.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Ivetic, may I then take it that you withdraw it as an associated exhibit, it already being in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, maybe my memory is failing me, but I thought we agreed that we would postpone the discussion of associated exhibit until after the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if an associated exhibit by mistake is presented as such, where that same document is already in evidence, then what still is relevant, Mr. Ivetic, is to establish that what is by mistake referred to as associated exhibit number so-and-so, that in reality is a reference to a document which is already in evidence, and I take it that you will take care of that during re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There's one more similar document. Can we please call up 1D02129.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now at paragraph 116 of your statement it begins: "I was shown a document, 65 ter 1D02129. The corps and brigade intelligence organs reported to us that Muslim forces were preparing a major offensive from the inner and outer ring in order to lift the blockade of Sarajevo." Now when I look at this document, it appears to a gazette entry recording President Karadzic's appointment of a War Presidency in Ilidza. It's on the screen before you. This is not the document you're referring to in paragraph 116, is it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 116 certainly doesn't speak about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So rather than me ask you any more questions about it, I'll leave it to Mr. Ivetic in his reopened direct examination to see if he can sort that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is time for the break. We'll ask for the witness to be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I think that yesterday we established already that there was no real chance to conclude the testimony of this witness today, but could you tell us how much time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe I'll still use the full six hours, Your Honour. I'm not sure how much time -- they tell me I've used about five hours so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that means that we'll also most likely not even conclude the cross-examination today. Since the Chamber has taken quite some time as well, we're the last ones to blame you for that situation. We take a break, and we resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be brought in, the Chamber would very much like the Defence to clear -- to thoroughly verify whether there are any other clerical errors, or whatever, in associated or non-associated exhibits. And, Mr. Groome, if you find some -- something that really makes no sense at all, because the document doesn't relate to anything the witness said, to already inform the Defence in advance so that they are still in a position to correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can provide some additional information as to the document that was dealt with before the break. Although I still have not been able to locate the document, in my binder I have the same document that Mr. Groome pulled up. But that evidence in the Karadzic statement related to Karadzic 65 ter number 1D6414. But again, I don't have that document to know where it is our system. I'll still have to look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, if you present this as evidence and then apparently not even knowing what it is about, let alone that the witness would have known about it, that, of course, is a mistake which certainly is not any less than not attaching a translation to a 65 ter document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let that be clear because it goes to content and not to form. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just on this point before we leave it. There's a voluminous number of documents with this witness so I haven't been able to check them all, although I have tried to check many. One other error that I see, which I would ask, encourage, Mr. Ivetic to examine over the break, for example, I think there are several documents, and one is in paragraph 103, where it refers -- the witness says something along the lines: "I have the same comment as I did to 1D8390." As far as I have been able to determine, that is not a document that's referred to in this witness statement. It is not a 65 ter number in this case, in the Karadzic case. I'm not sure where it comes from, but it might be useful to reexamine all of those cross-references because obviously when the witness is saying, "My evidence is the same about this," if we can't find the "this," we have no idea what his evidence is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I would like to add, Mr. Ivetic, that, of course, if the Defence wants the Chamber to carefully consider all the evidence, then this kind of error should be avoided to the extent possible because we usually go through all those documents attached to statements, et cetera. If we can't find them, that might become an obstacle. Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I want to draw your attention to paragraph 28 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And perhaps we could bring that up. It's D535 and paragraph 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In it you say that fire could only be opened on identified military targets and firing positions. You say: "We did not even return fire until we received permission from the superior command." My question to you is -- is very limited and very simply: Was this true throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And your reference to superior command, you're referring to the corps level -- the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say you sought permission before you fired, was this true for munitions of all calibres or only for munitions of a particular size and above or ...?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo, as a part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina theatre of war, was specific because often truce was fined [as interpreted] and even more often it was not -- the agreement was not honoured. So there were intermittent periods of truce and combat. Perhaps I can explain, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, my question is very specific now so -- and it relates to paragraph 28, where you say did you not return fire unless you received permission. So my question is limited to: Did that -- does your evidence apply to all calibres of weapons or just to some?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only calibres larger than 20 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So that calibres smaller than that, you did not and your subordinates did not seek permission to fire; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was standard procedure in place. If the forces of the ABiH army set out on a direct attack, it would have been absurd for me to ask permission to open fire. However, if there was sporadic fire which did not place our entire firing positions in danger, I would be informed what to do, and then the procedure was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, in essence, the procedure was where you can safely obtain advance permission, you should do so?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I now want to deal with another one of your associated exhibits and this is 1D02179. That's 1D2179. Now I want to deal with two documents that you give evidence about in paragraph 136 of your statement which reads: "These are documents of the Ilidza Brigade Military Police which obtained the necessary information in this case about our enemies in Hrasnica from Serbian civilians who had escaped." Before we look at the -- the documents in detail, I have a general question. These two documents you refer to in this paragraph, are they typical of the types of intelligence information which you had access to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have the statement on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was one of the ways for me to obtain enemy information. It was only one way from those Serbs who had fled from the other side and from some captured Muslims. I received such information from the organ for intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. And my question at this moment is: Do these two examples that have now been tendered through you as a witness, do they fairly represent the type of intelligence that you received about military targets?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just one or perhaps the first kind of gathering intelligence information and that information was then included into the puzzle I was putting together. The rule of thumb in an army is if you have two or three sources corroborating the same information, then it was safe to conclude that it was so. If there was only one or two, they had to be checked additionally. So we took all such single-source information with a grain of salt and carried out additional checks, as I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's take closer look now at 1D02179. In paragraph 136 of this report -- sorry, you now say in paragraph 136 that this report is from a Serbian civilian who escaped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you repeat the document number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's 1D02179. Let's take a look at what the document itself says.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In the first paragraph summarising the interview of Ilija Mocevic, it says: "His best man, Mensur Tenzo, persuaded him to join the so-called ARBiH where he stayed from 19 July 1992 until 5 December 1992. He left the so-called ABiH because, according to him, there were no Serbs in it or very few." So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the document number is 1D02179.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm perhaps starting to think that maybe it's not, Your Honour. Ms. Stewart does confirm that it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was not recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So I guess my question is your assertion in your statement that this person has escaped is simply not true. He didn't escape. He joined the ABiH, decided he didn't want to stay, and he left. That's the truth of what happened with this person; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on this statement, I can conclude that this man before the war lived in Hrasnica or Sokolovic Kolonija. When the roads were blocked, he remained there with his family. This best man of his, or a friend, probably with good intentions to keep him safe, advised him to join the ABiH. He left it after a while for the reasons he stated therein. It was not a unique case. There were many such cases in the 1st Corps of the ABiH. Those people were then later mobilised into so-called work platoons and used to dig trenches and carry out engineering works in risky areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I'd like to know about your source of knowledge. Do you know this person, this person which gave this statement, Mr. Mocevic? Do you know him personally and his personal circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you're telling us is your interpretation of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Based on this document you can see, more or less, how things developed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber can read the document and see what is stated in there, and if you have no personal knowledge about the circumstances, then is that what you add as information from, until now, rather general and unknown sources. Please proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the other document that you referred to in this -- in this paragraph. And this is 1D02180. Now, here we have another typical intelligence report. It reports to record [sic] information provided by Ognjen Damjanac. Now, I want to draw your attention to just below the middle of the paragraph containing Damjanac's information and read you a particular line from this quote -- from this: "The interviewee has not provided any information of interest except that he confirmed what we already know." So the person that interviewed Mr. Damjanac had the view that he did not provide information of interest; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you keep reading, you will get to an interesting part of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps you read the part that you found interesting.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll start reading from where you left it off. I lost the image. Perhaps it can be zoomed in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Don't touch the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Except that he confirmed what we already know. Meaning information. "The only thing he mentioned was that recently a work platoon from Hrasnica has been clearing up the area on Mount Igman, repairing communication trenches, and constructing the so-called grill covers. (Made of two layers of wooden logs with a layer of earth in between). So far they have built a cover about 300 metres long. He also confirmed that the command of the 4th Motorised Brigade had moved from Hrasnica to Sokolovic Kolonija and occupied the ground floor business premises opposite the Enker-Sokotrans warehouse." So there were pieces of information that we had not been able to corroborate before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, sir, this report is less than a month before the Hrasnica bombing. Were you aware that the command of the 4th Motorised Brigade had moved out of Hrasnica before you launched the air bomb into it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I known that, my intelligence officer would not have flagged this as new information. He did say he only mentioned something we know but then he added the information about communication trenches and the moving of the command. They probably moved their command post because of the air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, sir, this is -- this is before the air bomb. And now just to be clear, the command of the 4th Motorised Brigade was what you were referring to when you talked about the post office; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I still think --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So here we have intelligence, which you've said you used in determining where military targets were, that you had possession of intelligence three weeks before you fired the air bomb that the military target at the post office, the command, had moved; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say this. A brigade command is not the commander alone but everyone else and everyone -- everything else that accompanies him, including the communications centre of the 104th Motorised Brigade. A communication centre is a key element of command and control. The postal building made it possible for the commander to have it in place. Secondly, as a commander, I do not have only one command post. I have the main command post, a fake command post, and so on. This witness statement can be only relevant to the extent of indicating one such place where the brigade command may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it seems to indicate that at least as the post office is concerned, it was an empty command post. They had left.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR RADOJCIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never during the war was it empty. The communications centre was there throughout the war, and the other organs of the command were there throughout. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. I want to switch to a different topic and explore one of the targeting decisions that you made. Can we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the witness. Have you not now changed the military target the post office would have been from a command post to a communications centre? I think we earlier heard that it was because there was a command there and after being -- now having looked at documents which says that the command may not have been there any further, that you are saying: Well, it's still a communications centre, so that makes it a military target. Is that the shift from the one to the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no shift. The postal building was the basic, the main command post of the 104th Motorised Brigade throughout the war. In addition to that location, the commander had several forward command posts. In this specific case, he probably moved closer to the 2nd Sarajevo Brigade because of the forthcoming offensive. So perhaps he went to his forward command post number one, two or three. It is crystal-clear. I remain with my position. The postal building was the command post of the 104th Motorised Brigade throughout the war. The commander alone does not amount to an entire command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would direct your attention to transcript 47, lines 2 through 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, that sentence in this document which is on the screen says: "The command of the 4th Motorised Brigade ..." The command, not the commander. It doesn't say anything about a forward command post but "the command." Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. A fleeing Serb cannot be familiar with military tactics and what is contained as part of a single command. To him as a layperson, where the commander is is the command post. But to me who is familiar with it, that simply isn't true. I had three or four brigade command posts, depending on the focus of our activity, and the command post is not where the commander is only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have -- and I thank Mr. Ivetic for that. You earlier talked about the post office housing the command of the 104th Mechanised Brigade. Is that -- that's different from the command of the 4th Motorised Brigade, or is it ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 2004, there was a change of name for the units. The 4th became the 104th. The 2nd at Stup became the 102nd, and the 5th in the -- in Dobrinja, became the 155th. Hence, the difference in the statements. In any case, it is the same brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that in 2004 you said there was a change of name, or was it a different year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must have misspoken. 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the 4th and the 104th is actually the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Commanded by Fikret Prevljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we now have 1D02087 on our screens. It is an interim report authored by Colonel Radojcic dated the 14th of July, 1995.
